lessons.title: Preparing to grade groundnuts
lessons.html:
Why we grade groundnuts

Grading means checking a sample of groundnuts and giving it a grade according to the official grading regulations made under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990. The grade tells the buyer and the seller what the quality is, and it decides the price. A wrong grade costs the farmer or the silo money, and can lead to disputes. As a grader you must be accurate, honest and follow the method exactly.

Preparing for grading

  1. Make sure you have the current grading regulations and grade tables for groundnuts. The limits for each grade come from these tables, not from memory.
  2. Check your equipment: approved moisture meter (calibrated and checked), balance or scale (level, zeroed, checked with test weights), the prescribed sieves (clean, undamaged), sample divider, sorting tray, tweezers, containers and worksheets.
  3. Clean the work area so there is no grain or dust left from the previous sample.
  4. Wear a dust coat or overalls and a dust mask. Wash hands after grading, especially if grain may be treated or mouldy.

Taking and preparing the sample

  • Take the sample from the load at several points and depths with a probe, or from the automatic sampler, following the site procedure.
  • Mix the sample well and reduce it with the approved divider to the working sample size the procedure requires. Never pick a handful from the top.
  • Label the sample with the delivery or load number, date, time and your name.

Groundnuts are a food safety crop

Groundnuts can carry aflatoxin, a poison made by moulds. Mouldy, damaged and discoloured kernels are the biggest risk. Handle samples with gloves and a dust mask, and never taste or eat sample kernels.

lessons.title: Moisture and non-compliant material
lessons.html:
Determining moisture content

Moisture content is the percentage of water in the groundnuts. Grain that is too wet heats, goes mouldy and can be spoiled by insects. The regulations and the buyer set a maximum moisture level; check the current limit.

  1. Check that the moisture meter is set for groundnuts. Each grain has its own setting or calibration chart.
  2. Let the sample reach room temperature if the meter requires it; very hot or cold grain gives wrong readings.
  3. Fill the meter exactly as the manufacturer instructs and take the reading. Repeat if the procedure requires two readings.
  4. Record the reading on the worksheet immediately.
  5. If the reading is near the limit or the meter seems faulty, use the reference oven method or ask your supervisor.

Wet groundnuts in storage quickly grow mould and aflatoxin. Report any moist, warm or musty sample at once.

Determining non-compliant material

Next, weigh the working sample and separate the material that does not comply. Sort carefully on a clean tray. Put each kind in its own container and weigh it. Work out each as a percentage of the sample mass:

Percentage = mass of the material ÷ mass of the working sample × 100

Example: in a 100 g working sample you find 2.5 g of foreign matter. 2.5 ÷ 100 × 100 = 2.5%.

MaterialWhat to look for
Foreign matterSoil, stones, shells, sticks, plant parts
Mouldy kernelsKernels with visible mould, often green-yellow
Damaged kernelsInsect-damaged, heat-damaged, rotten or discoloured kernels
Split and broken kernelsHalves and pieces
Shrivelled or immature kernelsSmall, wrinkled, underdeveloped kernels
Poisonous seedsSeeds of poisonous weeds, as listed in the regulations

Mouldy kernels are kept and reported separately because they are linked to aflatoxin. A laboratory test for aflatoxin may be required.

lessons.title: Classifying groundnut seeds
lessons.html:
Classifying groundnut seeds

Besides grading, groundnuts are classified so that buyers know what type and size they are getting. The regulations and the buyer's specification say which classification is needed.

Type

Groundnut cultivars fall into groups such as Spanish types (smaller, round kernels, often used for peanut butter and confectionery) and Virginia types (larger, longer kernels, often used for roasting and snacks). Check that the sample matches the declared type. Kernels of another type in the sample may be a deviation.

Size

  1. Use the prescribed screens (sieves) for groundnut sizing.
  2. Shake the working sample through the screens as the method says.
  3. Weigh what stays on each screen and work out the percentages.
  4. Some buyers use a count: the number of kernels in a set mass. Count carefully and repeat if needed.

In-shell or kernels

Groundnuts may be delivered in-shell (in the pod) or as kernels (shelled). For in-shell samples, the procedure may require shelling a sub-sample to check the kernels inside and to work out the kernel percentage. Follow the site method.

Recording

Write the type, size results and any notes on the worksheet. Sound, mature kernels of the right type and size are worth the most. Lots with many small, mixed or damaged kernels may go to oil crushing instead of the edible market.

Good practice

  • Keep screens clean and undamaged; a bent screen gives wrong sizes.
  • Do not mix samples from different loads.
  • Use reference photographs to help decide difficult kernels.

lessons.title: Completing the grading process
lessons.html:
Completing the grading process

  1. Write every result on the worksheet: moisture and each deviation as a percentage.
  2. Compare each result with the grade table in the regulations. Start with the highest grade.
  3. The sample gets the highest grade for which all results are within the limits. If one result is over the limit for that grade, check the next grade.
  4. Check for conditions that make the groundnuts non-compliant or below grade regardless of percentages, such as a musty, sour or chemical smell, live insects, or poisonous seeds above the permitted level. Report these to your supervisor straight away.
  5. Sign the worksheet or enter the result in the system. The grade goes onto the delivery ticket or certificate.
  6. Keep the reference sample, sealed and labelled, for the period the site requires, in case of a dispute.

Cleaning up

Return the sample material as instructed, clean the sieves, trays and meter, and leave the work area clean for the next sample.

Honesty

Never change a result because a farmer or driver asks you to. If someone pressures you, call your supervisor. If you made a mistake, report it and re-grade.

Key points

  • Use the current grading regulations and calibrated equipment.
  • Take a representative sample and divide it properly.
  • Set the moisture meter for groundnuts and record readings straight away.
  • Percentage = mass of material ÷ sample mass × 100.
  • The grade is the highest grade for which all results comply.
